explanations.answer: Unspiritual and sold as a slave to sin
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul says the law is spiritual, then looks in the mirror and says, “…I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin.” He doesn't dress it up or hand himself a nicer title. Honest from the very first line, and I respect that.

explanations.answer: Spiritual and ready to keep the law
explanations.explanation: Close, but Paul hands the word "spiritual" to the law, not to himself. He says, “…the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual…” That little "but" is doing a lot of heavy lifting. Paul puts himself on the other side of it.

explanations.answer: Strong and free from the pull of sin
explanations.explanation: Oh, friend, Paul isn't walking in flexing here. He says he is “sold as a slave to sin.” Strong and free is the opposite of how he describes himself. This is a man being very honest about the struggle.

Not quite, baker, and Paul says it flat out. He writes, “For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do.” So he's doing the very things he hates and skipping the things he wants. It's the exact reverse of that statement.

Right, because Paul says the opposite. He writes, “I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do.” A man who did exactly what he wanted wouldn't be scratching his head like this. Paul is puzzled by himself, and that's the whole point of the verse.

Yes, good. Paul says, “And if I do what I do not want to do, I admit that the law is good.” Think about that. He's the one stumbling, and he still gives the law a clean report. He doesn't blame the law for his trouble.

Paul never calls the law unfair, friend. He does the opposite and says he admits “the law is good.” Even while he's tripping over his own feet, he keeps the law's name clean. The law isn't on trial in this verse.

Useless is a harsh word, and Paul doesn't touch it. He says that when he does what he doesn't want to do, “I admit that the law is good.” He agrees with the law even while he's struggling. That's some humility right there.

That's it. Paul says, “…it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.” He names sin as the one at work inside him. And he says it twice, in verse 17 and again in verse 20, so he really wants us to catch it.

Pride is a good guess, friend, but it's not the word on the page. Paul says, “…it is sin living in me that does it.” He names sin, plain and simple. The text doesn't mention pride anywhere in these verses.

Fear doesn't show up in this verse, baker. Paul says, “…it is sin living in me that does it.” That's the word he picks, and he repeats it again in verse 20. Hold onto sin, because it keeps coming back through the passage.
Not this time, friend. Paul says, “…I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out.” So the wanting is there. The carrying out is the part that gives him trouble.
That's right. Paul says, “…for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out.” He wants to do good, and he says so right there. The struggle is between the wanting and the doing.

explanations.answer: Evil is right there when he wants to do good
explanations.explanation: Yep. Paul says, “So this is the principle I have discovered: When I want to do good, evil is right there with me.” Every time he reaches for good, evil is standing next to him. He has gone around this loop a few times by now, and this is where he lands.

explanations.answer: Doing good gets easier the more he tries
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice discovery, wouldn't it? But it's not what Paul writes. He says, “When I want to do good, evil is right there with me.” Nothing in these verses says trying makes it easier. He just reports what he sees.

explanations.answer: Sin leaves him alone when he obeys the law
explanations.explanation: Nice idea, friend, but Paul says no such thing. He says, “When I want to do good, evil is right there with me.” So wanting to do good doesn't make evil step aside. It shows up right next to him.

Yes, delights. Paul says, “For in my inner being I delight in God’s law.” Don't miss that, baker. Right in the middle of all that struggle, there's real joy in him for God's law. That's the part of him that loves it.

Boasting doesn't fit this man at all, friend. Paul calls himself unspiritual and a slave to sin just a few verses back. What he says is, “For in my inner being I delight in God’s law.” Delight is the word, not boasting.

Rest sounds lovely, but it's not Paul's word here. He says, “For in my inner being I delight in God’s law.” Delight is joy, and he feels it deep down in his inner being. Notice he's still in the middle of a struggle, so rest isn't the picture.

That's right. Paul says he sees “another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind…” So there's a battle going on inside him. One side is the law of his mind, and the other side is working against it.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome, so I see why Rome came to mind. But this war isn't with any government. He says the other law is “warring against the law of my mind…” The fight is happening inside him.

The traditions of the elders don't come up anywhere in these verses, friend. Paul says the other law is “warring against the law of my mind…” This is a battle inside one man, not a debate over customs. Look at his mind, and you've found the target.

True, and it's a heavy line. Paul says this other law is “…holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me.” Captive is a strong word, and he picks it on purpose. Notice he describes where it lives, too: within him.
It's actually true, baker. Paul says the other law is “…holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me.” He really does use the word captive. That's how seriously he takes this struggle.

explanations.answer: Who will rescue him from this body of death
explanations.explanation: That's his question. Paul cries, “What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” He doesn't ask who will help him try harder. He asks who will rescue him, and that tells you he knows he can't pull himself out.

explanations.answer: Who will lift the weight of the law from him
explanations.explanation: Good try, friend, but Paul never talks about the law as a weight in this verse. In fact he has said the law is spiritual and good. What he asks is, “Who will rescue me from this body of death?” It's rescue he's calling for.

explanations.answer: Who will judge him for this war within
explanations.explanation: Judging isn't what Paul is asking for, baker. After calling himself wretched, he asks, “Who will rescue me from this body of death?” He's looking for a rescuer. And the very next verse, he gives thanks.

explanations.answer: God through Jesus Christ our Lord
explanations.explanation: Yes! Paul writes, “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!” Notice how fast it comes after his cry for a rescuer. He doesn't spend a long time wondering. He points straight to God and to Jesus.

explanations.answer: Moses who gave Israel the law
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, did have a big part with the law. John says, “For the law was given through Moses…” (John 1:17). But Paul doesn't thank Moses here. He says, “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!”

explanations.answer: Gamaliel who taught him the law
explanations.explanation: Gamaliel was a teacher of the law, and Paul tells us he was educated under him (Acts 22:3). But Paul doesn't thank him in this verse, friend. When he cries out for a rescuer, his thanks goes elsewhere: “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!”

Careful, friend, this one has the two switched around. Paul says, “…with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.” The mind goes with God's law. The flesh goes with the law of sin.

Right, the card flipped them. Paul says, “So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.” His mind serves God's law, and his flesh serves the law of sin. It's a tidy summary of the struggle he's been describing all along.
